newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices climb to new two month high.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices climb to new two month high.

text.p: World oil prices rallied strongly on Friday to a new two-month high, at the end of a bullish week where positive sentiment conquered negative supply and demand fundamentals.

In a burst of late trading the July futures contract for benchmark Brent blend crude oil settled at $20.35 a barrel, up 86 cents from the previous day's close. Earlier, it briefly touched $20.60, a level not seen since mid-March.
In New York NYMEX crude oil futures staged an equally strong late run to finish at $22.10 a barrel, up 80 cents.
Futures brokers said institutional funds had bought heavily into the New York market, which had helped push London higher.
The buying began late in the day and gathered a momentum of its own, hitting technical targets on the charts that graph the value of hydrocarbons, which triggered further purchasing.
The paper markets in London and New York set the levels from which most of the world's oil is priced.
Friday's late rise continued a crude oil rally begun last week that was driven initially by Middle East tension, technical factors, fund buying of futures and collective wish-fulfillment.

Its early peak was nearly $2 up at $19.72 on Monday. Most analysts said factors such as worry that Iraq's oil for food deal might not be renewed by the United Nations at the start of June were not sufficient to explain crude's strength.
A stream of news this week has underlined that throughout this summer more oil will be pumped from the world's reservoirs than can be consumed.
But the bearish news has had litte effect on crude prices, which remained steady through the week until Friday's gallop forward.
The rise was first kicked off last week by industry rumours that maintenance programmes would cut deeply into supplies of North Sea crude in June.
The fears proved exaggerated, even though in June some 12.5 million barrels less oil will be marketed from the North Sea than in May. Dealers said they had been expecting a bigger impact.
With doubt over loading programmes no longer supporting higher prices, oil traders had begun to question how long crude's rally could last.

Refined oil products have not enjoyed the same rise in price as the crude from which they are distilled. As a consequence refinery operators have seen their profit margins massacred, and that was expected to pressure values.
"Everyone expects crude to come off, but will it be a week, or two or three, that's what nobody knows," said one product trader, complaining crude's strength has slowed his business almost to a halt.
"We have to see further positive action in the products or the current crude rally will fail," said Leslie Nicholas, energy analyst at GNI Research. "The implications of that are obvious."
Crude dropped sharply earlier this year from $25 to around $18 as poor winter demand failed to soak up a flood of extra material.
Analysts began to talk in the early spring of crude values returning to the $13 to $18 range prevalent before last summer.
The recent rally has thrown those predictions off course, with the latest upswing leaving them looking even further off the mark.
